Russian transport police detained him after the plane landed safely in St Petersburg, prosecutor Alexander Bebenin told reporters at the city's Pulkovo airport. Bebenin said the man had threatened to blow up the plane if his demands of diverting the flight to Strasbourg were not met.

Passengers overpowered him after he had handed a note to attendants with his demands, he said. No explosives were found on the passenger or the plane, he said.

The man, whose identity has not been disclosed, is a native of Uzbekistan, Turkish and Russian officials have said. Bebenin said he was a Russian citizen, but Turkey's civil aviation authority head Ali Ariduru said that he was an Uzbek citizen.

Most of the passengers aboard the flight were unaware of the hijack attempt and only found out on emerging from the plane after a two-hour wait on the tarmac, Bebenin said.

Heading: US Senate asked to finance upgrade of Pakistani F-16s - Indian Express
Content:
At least 52 LTTE cadres and five soldiers were killed as heavy fighting raged on Wednesday for control of the key Northern Sri Lankan city of Kilinochchi with government forces pressing fighter aircraft to pound tiger bunkers on the outskirts.

Fighter jets went into action this morning hitting LTTE bunkers and other concentrations on the town's periphery in two air raids, air force spokesman Wing Commander Janaka Nanayakkara said.

He said the jets targeted the LTTE heavy vehicles summoned to the location to drag away the damaged earth moving vehicles which tigers were using for constructing new defences.

In ground clashes, troops on the Kilinochchi front gained ground in Vannerikulam on Tuesday with the defence ministry stating that 10 LTTE cadres were killed and six others wounded in the incident.

The ministry said four soldiers also lost their lives in these confrontations.

Government troops had three separate confrontations in the Vannerikkulam area and reported killing three tiger rebels while six soldiers were injured.

The government forces are advancing into Kilinochchi in several pincers and are reported to be just two to three kilometres from the town.

Another Lankan task force hit the LTTE concentration areas near Madamoddai on Tuesday, the ministry said adding 10 tiger cadres were killed and many others injured.

Army snipers deployed in the forward area said four LTTE cadres were shot dead during the day, the ministry said. Separately, 57th division troops, spearheading the assault on Kilinochchi, carried out a series of attacks at LTTE positions located in the east and the west of the town, the military said, adding 14 tiger rebels were reported killed in the incidents.

In another incident, troops of the same division heading towards Mankulam from the west of the region attacked a group of LTTE cadres traveling on a tractor on Tuesday afternoon. At least four LTTE cadres were killed in the incident, the Defence Ministry said adding in a similar attack carried out later in the afternoon, troops confirmed an LTTE cadre was killed.

In a separate confrontation reported from the north of Mankulam area around 12.40 pm, troops claimed two Tamil tigers were killed.

At least one tiger rebel was shot dead in Nallikulam in Vavuniya in another confrontation on Tuesday, the ministry said.

On the Mullaittivu front, troops of 59 division conducted day-long offensives in the Andankulam, Thannimurippukulam, Nayaru and Kiriibbanwewa areas.

One LTTE cadre and a soldier were killed in the incident, the ministry said. Troops also engaged in mine-clearing operations removed 45 AP mines and six improvised explosive devices (IEDs) during the day.

Separately, troops killed two LTTE cadres in the Illuppakadavali in Mannar region on Tuesday, the officials said, adding two soldiers were injured in a claymore mine attack at Pottani in Batticaloa on the same day.

Heading: Eight Indian-Canadians elected to Parliament - Indian Express
Content:
The US administration has held a special briefing to persuade Senate staffers to help finance the mid-life upgrade of Pakistan's ageing fleet of F-16 combat jets in the face of opposition to the move in the Congress.

US Assistant Secretary of State Richard Boucher, who looks after South Asian affairs at the State Department, briefed the staffers, telling them that upgrading the F-16s would increase Pakistan's effectiveness in the war against terror. Pakistan has a total of 34 F-16s purchased mostly in the 1980s and the jets are currently in need of a mid-life upgrade to retain their combat effectiveness. In recent weeks, the military has used the F-16s to target Taliban hideouts in the troubled Bajaur tribal region.

The US government has already accepted Pakistan's request to refurbish the aircraft by equipping them with modern technology and weapon systems to make them comparable with newer versions of the F-16s. The mid-life upgrade will cost a $891 million. Pakistan agreed to pay $417 million and asked the US to provide the remaining $474 million, the Dawn newspaper reported on Wednesday.

The proposal is strongly resisted in the US Congress. Lawmakers say that Pakistan does not need F-16s to fight terrorists. They have argued that Pakistan needs financial support to revive its economy and not for buying F-16s.

They also say that given the country's economic situation, Pakistan may fail to pay its share for upgrading the aircraft, thus forcing the US to bear all the expenses.

In July, the US State Department notified a Senate committee that it had accepted Pakistan's request to make available $226 million from the foreign military finance programme for upgrading the F-16s.

The US administration needs Congress's permission to provide the remaining amount.

Heading: Polish leaders fight over EU summit - Indian Express
Content:
Eight Indian-Canadians, including seven sitting MPs have been elected to the Canadian Parliament in the elections that saw Prime Minister Stephen Harper-led Conservative Party winning, albeit short of a majority.

Tim Uppal, who won from the Alberta province will join for the first time the other Indian-origin MPs, who have been re-elected to the new House. Deepak Obhrai, Ruby Dhalla and Gurbax Singh Malhi, besides Navdeep Bains, Ujjal Dosanjh, Nina Grewal and Ratan Singh are the members who have been re-elected.

In 2006, 10 Indian-Canadians were elected to Parliament compared with three Arabs and five Chinese.

Thanking her supporters following the victory, Conservative MP Nina Grewal, who was re-elected to Fleetwood-Port Kells in a landslide victory said she was pleased with the result despite it resulting in another minority government.

"I worked so hard for the people of Fleetwood-Port Kells; my work speaks for itself," she said. Grewal, who was the first Indo-Canadian woman elected to the House of Commons in 2004, won by a slim margin in the last election.

Malhi, who in 1993 became the first turbaned MP in Canada, won for the sixth time from Bramalea-Gore-Malton. Bains also won easily for the third time in Mississauga-Brampton South.

In British Columbia province, former Canadian health minister Ujjal Dosanjh won in Vancouver South.

Heading: UK may set up telecom database to fight crime - Indian Express
Content:
Poland's Prime Minister has denied the country's President a Government flight to prevent him from attending an European Union summit in a struggle for power in Warsaw.

The world may be facing its biggest economic crisis in 80 years, but for the past weeks Polish leaders have locked horns repeatedly over who should represent the biggest ex-communist EU newcomer at the summit on Wednesday and Thursday.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk has argued he is entitled to lead the Polish delegation unless he picks someone else, but conservative President Lech Kaczynski said he was going to Brussels no matter what.

Tusk appeared to gain the upper hand ahead of the summit, coming to Brussels on Tuesday evening in a Government plane, which he refused to send back to Warsaw to fetch the President. Kaczynski was scrambling to charter a plane on Wednesday morning, Polish news media reported.

The Government-controlled Foreign Ministry has not secured for the President a badge allowing him to enter the summit building, but diplomats said the leader was unlikely to be turned away if he showed up at a last moment.

"This does not look serious — as if there were not more important things to quarrel about," said an EU diplomat.

The Polish media have compared the leaders to boys fighting over toys in a sand-pit.

The Government feels the presence of Kaczynski could spoil Warsaw's delicate diplomacy aimed at watering down the EU's plan to fight the climate change.

Heading: RBI, FM leave banks flush with funds - Indian Express
Content:
In the backdrop of the airline industry demand for a Rs 4,750 crore bailout package, Civil Aviation Minister Praful Patel expressed disappointment over the approach of some ministries on sops for the sector.

"We need a consensus," Patel said, regretting that "many departments are not taking a positive approach."

Taxes on ATF and charges for aviation services, he said, could be eased to help airlines fly out of the crisis fuelled by high jet fuel costs and the world economic slowdown. But the government is awaiting the recommendations of an official panel in this regard.

Heading: As CBI chief he moved against Maya, now parent cadre UP sits on NOC to grant him pension - Indian Express
Content:
India today announced a multi-pronged aggressive plan to lubricate the banking system with copious liquidity, get more foreign capital inflows and smoothen credit to the corporate sector. Significantly, it also picked cues from the United States and Europe by deciding to infuse up to Rs 4,000 crore capital into state-owned and private banks to make them more robust in times of global financial instability.

What remains is a cut in the signal repo rate that will boost the investment climate and prod companies to go ahead with their spending plans for the next fiscal. A 50 basis point cut in the repo rate cut may be announced by Reserve Bank of India Governor Duvvuri Subbarao on October 24 when he presents the monetary policy for the busy season.

The announcements by the Finance Ministry and the RBI were made after the stock markets closed. The 30-scrip benchmark Sensex lost 674 points or almost 6 per cent to end at 10,809. The confidence building measures are expected to weigh favourably on the markets when it opens tomorrow.

The RBI cut the cash reserve ratio (the portion of deposits banks keep with the RBI) by 100 basis points to 6.5 per cent and released Rs 40,000 crore more funds to banks. With today's cut, total liquidity injected into the system by relaxing the CRR is a whopping Rs 100,000 crore (it was cut 150 bps last week).

Banks have also been allowed to borrow 0.5 per cent of their deposits parked in government securities towards meeting statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) norms by pledging these as collateral with the RBI. This will be only for meeting the needs of mutual funds facing redemption pressure. The 0.5 per cent cut in SLR (the portion of deposits banks invest in government securities) is over and above the 1 per cent cut announced exactly a month ago to extend liquidity support to banks. Effectively, the SLR for banks now stands at 23.5 per cent.

Earlier, Finance Minister P Chidambaram said the government would release Rs 25,000 crore to banks and financial institutions under the Agricultural Debt Waiver and Debt Relief Scheme. The RBI, he said, will provide Rs 7,500 crore to commercial banks and another Rs 17,500 crore to Nabard.

To encourage foreign capital inflows, the Finance Ministry doubled the amount foreign institutional investors (FIIs) can invest in corporate bonds to $ 6 billion. The interest rate ceiling on Foreign Currency Non-Resident deposits of all maturities and on Non-Resident (External) Rupee Account have also been hiked by 50 basis points to make them more attractive and bring home more foreign inflows. For FCNR (B), it translates into an interest rate of Libor plus 25 bps and for NR(E)RA, Libor plus 100 bps.

Today's measures are significant in that they address several problems. One, by liberalising foreign capital inflows, the government and the RBI hope the rupee will appreciate some bit on its own without requiring intervention. The central bank has been aggressively selling dollars (in other words buying rupees and sucking liquidity) to stem volatility in the foreign exchange market and hold the rupee from breaching the psychological 50 to a dollar mark.

Two, it infused enough liquidity to ease the situation in the overnight money markets where interest rates had zoomed to 20 per cent plus last week. The CRR cut had, in one way, become inevitable since the banks continued to borrow huge sums of Rs 70,000 crore and Rs 62,800 crore through the repo window of the RBI on Monday and Tuesday respectively even after last week's 150 bp cut.

The RBI issued an advisory to banks to actively extend term loans and working capital to Indian corporates. Given the tight monetary conditions, many banks were reluctant to lend and some even saw an opportunity to make quick money by lending at very high rates in the call money market. It also plans to set up Special Market Operations (SMOs) for oil bonds as it had done for public sector oil marketing companies in June-July 2008.

The measures boosting liquidity will now encourage banks to lend more to the corporate sector, which is forced to borrow more domestically because the external commercial borrowing window remains virtually shut for rupee expenditure to non-infrastructure companies.

Banks have also been allowed to borrow funds from their overseas branches and correspondent banks up to a limit of 50 per cent of their unimpaired Tier I capital as at the close of the previous quarter or $10 million, whichever is higher, as against the existing limit of 25 per cent.

Heading: Muslim policemen removed from Advani duty, Kerala orders probe - Indian Express
Content:
It has been almost a year since the CBI applied for a no-objection certificate to initiate the process for pension benefits to Vijay Shanker but the Uttar Pradesh government is still sitting on the request, denying post-retirement benefits to the former CBI Director. It was under his tenure that the CBI processed the disproportionate assets case against Chief Minister Mayawati.

Vijay Shanker retired on July 31 this year after a service extension. A 1969 batch IPS officer, he belonged to the UP cadre. So when his retirement date neared, the CBI, sources said, put in a request last November for an NOC from the UP government — the service extension hadn't been announced then. But the UP government, the sources said, is still to grant the certificate. This has delayed grant of pension benefits to the former Director.

Vijay Shanker was still heading the agency when the CBI had made a submission in court in the disproportionate assets case involving Mayawati. This led to a storm with Mayawati accusing the CBI of allowing itself to be used by the Centre to settle political scores. She subsequently withdrew support to the Congress-led UPA government. Even during the trust vote in Lok Sabha, BSP MPs referred to the CBI submission and alleged that the UPA government tried to threaten Mayawati intobacking it.

Heading: ‘Dark side of India’ gets Adiga Booker - Indian Express
Content:
The much-feared shakeout in the Indian aviation industry began to hit home on Wednesday as hundreds of employees of leading private airline Jet Airways took to the streets in protest after they were fired overnight, a move the company said was in the greater interest of regaining viability and security its economic health.

While the company said it had "released" 800 flight attendants recruited recently for Jet's planned expansion programme, it added another 1,100 employees to that list later in the day and said they would include probationary and unconfirmed personnel in other areas including cockpit crew and management personnel.

Aviation industry sources said that this seemed like the beginning of a bloodletting in the sector and other airlines, including Vijay Mallya's Kingfisher Airlines which joined hands with Jet only two days ago to share facilities and cut costs, could follow suit. Kingfisher last month sacked 300 employees, many of them from Air Deccan with which it merged earlier this year. A top Kingfisher official, however, told The Indian Express that it was "very premature for anybody to jump to a conclusion that it would lay off employees just because Jet had done so".

"It is an unfortunate decision, which all of us in the company regret but it is an attempt to save the company and the jobs of the remaining employees," Jet Airways Executive Director B Saroj Dutta told a news conference at the airline's headquarters in Mumbai.

Airlines around the world have been hit hard by rising oil prices and falling traffic, which has been compounded by the global financial crisis. While state-run Air-India posted a loss of over Rs 2,100 crore in 2007-08, Kingfisher's losses were over Rs 1,000 crore and that of Jet over Rs 800 crore during the same period. Domestic traffic fell by 5.3 per cent in August to 29.2 lakh from 31 lakh in July.

But all that is little consolation to the hundreds of laid-off Jet employees who protested outside its office, many in their golden yellow uniforms who shouted slogans demanding their jobs back. "We've done nothing wrong," said Mitesh Bhatt, who joined Jet in January and was about to complete his probation.

Similar sentiments were expressed by his colleagues who sounded helpless at the loss. "I joined Jet in April this year and did not give my first year BA exams as the joining date was earlier. They have played with our future as no airline will now take us," said Vishav Preet from Amritsar.

The crisis took a political turn as the laid off employees marched to the office of the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena and sought the intervention of its chief Raj Thackeray. He did not disappoint them and threatened that no Jet flight would be allowed to operate if the employees were not reinstated.

"A delegation had come to meet us. We heard them and think that they should not have been laid off without any warning, explanation or compensation. We will be meeting the company officials tomorrow and the next course of action will be decided," said MNS spokesman Nitin Sardesai.

Officials of the Shiv Sena's labour wing, the Bhartiya Kamgar Sena, also held talks with the Jet Airways management through the day. "Of the 1,000 odd employees laid off by Jet airways, there were 578 from Mumbai. They were on probation and not permanent employees. Though they are not registered with our union, we have taken up their matter with the management. The management has given us in writing that these employees will be taken back on priority once they get more flights. We will, however, keep a vigil and have asked the management not to do the same with permanent employees," said Vinayak Raut, Bharatiya Kamgar Sena secretary. The Left trade union CITU slammed the Jet move as "illegal and atrocious" and sought the government's intervention. It demanded grounding of all flights.

(with inputs from Swatee Kher)

Heading: Singur-larly good options - Indian Express
Content:
Not everyone quits a job to think up a story of a rickshawpuller's son who writes letters to "Mr Premier" Wen Jiabao over seven days. Not everyone wins the Man Booker Prize at the age of 33. Aravind Adiga has done both; the second he has managed by a whisker — he turns 34 a week from now on October 23.

After his debut novel, The White Tiger, won the Booker for 2008 and 50,000 pounds, Adiga, uncharacteristically beaming in a tux in London, said, "The first thing I'm going to do is find a bank I can put it in. I'm serious!" And then turned characteristically serious: "It was important for me to present someone from the colossal underclass, which is perhaps as big as 400 million, and to do so without sentimentality."

In Booker's 40th year, Adiga — the second youngest winner after Ben Okri, who won in 1991 aged 32 — bested fellow Indian Amitav Ghosh, Australian Steve Toltz, Irishman Sebastian Barry and Britons Linda Grant and Philip Hensher.

Michael Portillo, chairman of the five-member judging panel, gave the reason. "My criterion was 'does it knock my socks off?' and this one did," he said. "What set this one apart was its originality. For many of us this was entirely new territory — the dark side of India."

Adiga's hero Balram Halwai sees Delhi, driving around in a Honda City. Three years ago, in his previous life as a journalist with Time magazine, Adiga too wandered, not in a car, picking up material for the book.

"In Delhi, I travelled a lot by bus and autorickshaw, and spoke to as many drivers and conductors as I could — they are the sources for many of the things Balram says in the book," Adiga said. "He is a composite of many people whom I've encountered in many travels."

And travelled he has. Born in Chennai and brought up in Mangalore, Adiga left with his family for Sydney when he was 16. Then came a Bachelors degree at Columbia University and a Masters at Oxford, before he went back to New York as a business journalist. How did a doctor's son, who dreamt all along of becoming a writer, end up pacing Wall Street? "I did not want to continue in academics. The only job that could use a person with no skills but those provided by an English Masters was journalism," he laughed. "I became a business journalist mostly out of necessity —- no other jobs were available at the time —- but it proved to a rewarding experience, by exposing me to economics, the stock market and other such financial and economic aspects of living."

Adiga came to New Delhi in 2003 as Time's correspondent, a job he quit in late 2005. That was the year Chinese premier Wen visited Bangalore, and Adiga began his novel. "There is a real historical hook to the opening," Adiga said. "I wanted things in the book to correspond to reality, but filtered through Balram's views. India and China are supposed to take over the world this century —- or so we keep hearing in the press —- so I thought it would be nice to present a narrative that acknowledges that apparent takeover of the world and treats it ironically."

A few months after The White Tiger was released, Adiga suspected HarperCollins, his publisher in India, was making up sales figures. He need not worry anymore. All he needs now is a way to deal with his fame —- and some solitude to finish his second novel. (With agency inputs)

Heading: Winners keepers - Indian Express
Content:
Acquiring land in India is no easy business, as the Singur crisis showed. Here is another way. In today's circumstances, lets assume that, say, Reliance plans an oil pipeline that needs contiguous areas of land. If any one of the landowners in the path of the pipeline holds out, the project will not take off, leaving Reliance with several non-contiguous pieces of land and a large hole in their pocket. In an alternative scenario, instead of buying any plot of land, Reliance could choose to buy an option from the landowner. The option will give Reliance the right to buy the land at the prevailing market (or agreed upon) price within a period of three years (for instance). This option can be valued using simple decision analysis tools in a matter of minutes, and would be an order of magnitude cheaper than acquiring the land itself. Reliance could then plan multiple pipeline routes and try to acquire options on each of the routes. The moment they have all the options on a particular route, they can exercise all the options on that route and acquire all the contiguous pieces of land.

There are several benefits to this approach. First, as Reliance is a private party, they are not required to reveal the purpose of the acquisition. They can send out agents who don't even need to reveal that Reliance is behind the acquisition. The government, on the other hand, is required to reveal the purpose of their acquisition, resulting in landowners realising that they can make a lot of money if they hold out. The cost of acquisition will now be based on a good deal between the private party and the landowner. Second, as exercising the option is a legal right, there is no necessity for state coercion of the individual landowner. If someone holds out even after selling an option, that will be considered contractual fraud, and we have a legal framework in place to deal with that. The government no longer needs to deal with mass protests, the police no longer needs to open fire on hostile crowds, and entrepreneurs no longer need to sink large sums of money in legal costs. Third, if some people (tribals, farmers, or the middle class) have a strong connection to their land and don't want to leave it, all they have to do is not sell the option to their land. There should be no legal authority on the part of the government or the industry to force them to do so, and any forcible or fraudulent activity on the part of the entrepreneur would be subject to our existing legal framework that prohibits fraud and coercion. Human rights organisations can shift their focus from protesting to educating tribals and farmers about their options.

If this method is so simple, why hasn't it been tried already? Well, it has — it just hasn't been spoken about, as most private firms don't want to talk about their land acquisition strategy. It's said that Disney used options to acquire most of the land they needed for their theme park at Anaheim, California. Disney saved a fortune in legal fees by using this method. What works in the United States may not necessarily work in India, but I have anecdotal evidence that Larsen and Toubro, in the construction of the third Howrah bridge in West Bengal, offered such a good deal in Dakshineshwar, that neighbouring land owners requested L&T to consider buying their land too.

There are some legitimate challenges to this solution, especially in places like West Bengal where the business climate is highly interventionist, with entrepreneurs unable to operate without the blessings of the local politicians. But the government needs to realise that it cannot replace coercive prevention of industry by coercive adoption of it — it needs to shrink to a minimal form of government. Using the options system is far less coercive, while at the same time providing industry and farmers with that rarest of commodities —informed choice.

The writer is doing a PhD in decision and risk analysis, Stanford University

Heading: An absolute advantage - Indian Express
Content:
The editorial in the latest issue of the Organiser is titled "Nano in Gujarat". It observes: "The Tatas choosing Gujarat need not have hit headlines. But Ratan Tata choosing Gujarat after a wasted, controversial and disappointing experience in West Bengal has created history... Tatas is not like any other corporate house in the country. It is truly the pride of India. It has built a reputation unique for itself over many decades and it is widely acknowledged as the benchmark of corporate ethics. The Tatas has grown to occupy its position as the most-reputed corporate national entity and Indian multinational company by upholding character, professionalism, grit and vision. It was with this élan and business acumen that Tatas chose Gujarat. It is, rather, homecoming."

It adds: "Equally significant is the context and the host. When Tatas went to West Bengal to set up its dream project it was really ground-breaking and adventurous. Marxists are not known to be entrepreneur savvy. In three decades the Left has ensured that the state became a graveyard of industries. From being the number one industrial state in the country West Bengal under the Marxists decayed to an abyss of poverty, illiteracy, backwardness and flight of talent. Buddhadeb tried to change the format in a crude, arrogant, top-down-type Chinese way. But that Tatas decided to go to Singur immensely raised the Marxist Chief Minister's stock and perhaps it played a major part in his unprecedented victory in the last assembly election. Mamata Banerjee's obstinacy and the CPM's obduracy demolished it all—Gujarat Chief Minister Narendra Modi is the winner in the bargain."

Nuclear servitude

A two-page spread titled "Deal capped our right to test and tied India to NPT" reproduces RSS chief K S Sudarshan's Vijayadashmi speech In Nagpur. The RSS chief noted: "It will be better if the Prime Minister, instead of making controversial decisions, concentrates on curbing the bane of terrorism which will be backed by the whole nation. What is the message he is sending by not executing the perpetrator of terror-blasts?... If all of us move in unison, tread our own respective paths cooperating with each other then the day is not far away when the flag of our nation will fly highest in the world. ''

On the 123 Indo-US nuclear deal, he observed: "In case India goes for nuclear test it would result in 'most serious consequences' including immediate cut off of nuclear-fuel, its technology and the supply of atomic reactors. In spite of all this, if the Prime Minister thinks that Bharat has got a waiver for atomic test then it means that he considers the people of Bharat as fools. The logical conclusion is that Bharat has mortgaged its right to conduct nuclear tests and bound itself with Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT)."

Appeasement politics

In his column tilted "An Indian parallel in appeasement politics in the US," Organiser editor R. Balashankar observes: "The global financial crisis might largely be the outcome of the incompetence and greed of the private sector. Many experts in the US however blame the government for its mindless affirmative action at the root of the mortgage crisis. If it is true India is also fast slipping into a similar situation. As in the US, in India too some of the actions of the government have all the potential to create a financial disaster. The Manmohan Singh government has crossed all permissible limits in budget deficit by its various poll-oriented populist schemes like loan waiver and subsidy. The real attack on the health of the financial system has come in the form of affirmative action with the pledge of giving minorities the 'first right' in national resources. The sincerity of this statement is widely doubted. But the manner in which the government implemented it raised many eyebrows."

Compiled by Suman K Jha

Heading: The great thawing - Indian Express
Content:
Economists are obsessed with elegance. Their bodies might be proportioned more like refrigerators or lampposts than ballerinas, but that is of no consequence. To an economist, elegance lies in a description of human behaviour that is at once explanatory, predictive, and parsimonious. This is a little like building a recognisable model of the world with as few Lego blocks as possible. The best economists are able to refine our view of this world by adding or removing just a few blocks. Paul Krugman, the 2008 Nobel laureate in economics and a giant in the theory of international trade, is such an economist.

Krugman has received this award early, at the age of 55. But precocity has been a consistent feature of his professional life. He completed his PhD in just three years. When he received his degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1977, he had already done much of the work that was to make him famous. He has taught at several top economics departments, including long stretches at MIT and Princeton. In 1991, he was recognized as the best American economist under 40 when he received the John Bates Clark Medal.

Krugman has also made notable forays outside academia. He served on the Council of Economic Advisors during the Reagan administration, has written several popular books on economics, and is now an unabashedly liberal columnist for The New York Times. Yet, it is unlikely that he could have achieved any of this was it not, as the Nobel Committee described it, "for his analysis of trade patterns and location of economic activity."

To get a better sense of Krugman's contributions to economics, we need to make a brief stop in early 19th century England. In response to rising domestic prices of food grain, independent traders had begun importing wheat and corn. While this was welcomed by many, landowners were understandably displeased. Their agricultural profits went down, and they were forced to reduce expenditure on essential items such as wigs. However, landowners eventually took advantage of their majority in parliament to enact the "Corn Laws", which effectively banned imports of food grain.

One of the loudest voices in opposition to the Corn Laws was that of David Ricardo, now recognized as the father of theoretical economics. Despite his own considerable land-holdings (the result of a successful career in stockbroking), Ricardo was committed to reopening trade. Two of his insights from that period have been immensely influential in modern economics. The first is the idea that abstraction is a useful tool. Ricardo's arguments were based on a vision of a world stripped down to the bare essentials: a few "types" of individuals who differed in preferences and endowments, and well-defined markets in which they interacted. The logical clarity that comes from mathematical abstraction is now the trademark of economic theory, for better or for worse.

Ricardo's second insight was more specific: when countries specialise production according to "comparative advantage", they are (generally) made better off. Suppose that, in India, it takes one worker to produce a bushel of corn and two workers to produce a wig. Also suppose that in England, it takes ten workers to produce a bushel of corn and five workers to produce a wig. In this case, India has a comparative advantage in corn and England has a comparative advantage in wigs (even though India has an absolute advantage in both). Ricardo's argument, reinforced and formalised by many economists since then, is that both India and England will gain if India exports corn to England and England exports wigs to India.

This is a powerful idea with far-reaching implications for global welfare. While critics of globalisation have valid concerns (such as the difficulty of distributing the gains from trade and the short-run costs of reallocating labour), their reluctance to acknowledge the fundamental wisdom of comparative advantage has put them at a comparative disadvantage in the academic discourse.

When Krugman was in graduate school, there was concern that some patterns of trade could not be explained by this theory. Why do nearly identical countries trade in nearly identical goods? For example, Germany exports BMWs to Sweden while Sweden exports Saabs to Germany. Shouldn't the country with a comparative advantage in cars produce both BMWs and Saabs? And if neither has a comparative advantage, why doesn't each produce its own BMWs and Saabs?

Krugman showed, in a ten-paged paper, that two very simple modifications to the theory could explain this and more. First, consumers like having choices over similar goods (Saabs and BMWs, for example). Second, there are economies of scale. In other words, the more Saabs a country produces, the lower the average cost of making each Saab. In this setting, even if Germany and Sweden were identical (in that neither had a comparative advantage in car production), it would make sense for each to specialize across brands. Allowing Sweden to produce all Saabs and Germany to produce all BMWs keeps the average cost of each car lower than if trade was blocked.

Krugman built on these insights to expand and improve theories not only of international trade but also economic geography. This is the study of where and how labour and capital are distributed. Thanks to his research, we now have a clearer understanding of the mechanisms through which cities might or might not emerge as centers of production. Krugman's arguments are brilliant because they are so stark and simple that they seem obvious. This is the trademark of many great inventions, from the wheel to the Sudoku puzzle.

While the decision to award the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to Paul Krugman is certainly appropriate, it will come as a disappointment to Indians that the prize was not shared with Jagdish Bhagwati and Avinash Dixit. Both Bhagwati and Dixit have written seminal papers that have deeply influenced Krugman's research, and several economists had predicted a three-way award.

That this did not happen is perhaps in part due to Krugman's notoriety as a columnist. Krugman is unique among economists for the vehemence of his political positions. He has the distinction of being one the most provocative commentators in the mainstream American media. While his reasoned arguments for greater redistribution and undisguised support for the Democratic party have won him many enemies, economists should also be grateful to him for showing that the necessary amorality of the discipline does not necessitate silence on the ethical issues of the day.

The writer teaches economics at the University of Chicago

Heading: Rising Sensex slips on liquidity fears - Indian Express
Content:
Syria has recognised Lebanese sovereignty for the first time in six decades. This is a momentous change of tone for Bashar al-Assad's leadership, and mirrors larger changes in the Middle East region, explains Alia Allana.

 

•Why was Syria in Lebanon?

Syrian presence in Lebanon was a result of the Lebanese Civil War which lasted 15 years. Following this period, Syria continued to exert influence and maintained a presence in Lebanon, influencing both domestic and foreign policy. This retreat comes in the face of growing criticism of Syria's role in Lebanon from both regional and international players.

 

•What changes have occurred in the Middle East to herald such a move?

The first major change in Syria arises from its attempted reconciliation with Israel attempting to end the age-old rivalry between the two powers. In May 2008, Syria and Israel both announced informal peace-talks which had been brokered by the Turkish government. Talks are currently underway in Cairo regarding the Arab-Israeli peace process. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has emphasised the key role Syria plays in this region and the need for its support.

•Syria is on the list of states that sponsor terrorism; why?

Syria has been linked to the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah. Hezbollah's aims are to "liberate lands that have remained occupied" by Israel and to protect Lebanon from Israeli occupation. Israeli PM has responded by saying that they have "no intention" of attacking Lebanon or Syria. Syria has been placed on this list by the US due to several reasons other than Hezbollah — Syria has allegedly bought nuclear technology illegally from North Korea; it has a very close relationship with Iran (US State Dept)and there are allegations that Syria was behind the death of Lebanese president and reformer Rafiq Hariri.

 

•Syria-Israel peace-talks counter the Bush administration's strategy to isolate Syria; what has been the impetus behind these developments?

Middle Eastern powers have recognized the volatility in the region and have decided to take matters in their own hands irrespective of the policies of the Bush administration. This might lead to positive change, because Israel has approached both Syria and Lebanon. Both Syria and Lebanon need to be taken on board, because if one allies with the Israel and the other does not, there is potential for further conflict in the area.  

 

•How crucial is US support for peace in the Middle East?

A peace process without US support might not yield much result, and communication between the Syrian and US governments is very limited — there is however the possibility of talks at the French-sponsored Euro-Mediterranean in Paris. This is where the Israeli and Syrian heads of states will talk face to face, for the first time in the history of the two countries.

Heading: Banks to get Rs 4,000 crore capital boost - Indian Express
Content:
Snapping a two-day rally, stocks again plunged on the back of worsening liquidity in the money market, and looming global recession. Weak cues from the world's stock markets and intense selling pressure shaved 674.28 points, or 5.87 per cent, off the Sensex. But investors can take hope from the cash reserve ratio (CRR) cut that was announced after markets closed for trading. The Reserve Bank of India's decision is expected to have a positive effect on markets and stocks may rise tomorrow.

As the RBI extension for banks' special short-term lending (repo) facility to mutual funds was unable to lift investor sentiments, the Sensex ended at 10,809.12 points on Wednesday. The central bank said it would conduct a special 14-day repo auction for Rs 16,500 crore to enable banks to meet liquidity needs of mutual funds. On Tuesday, just four banks bid for Rs 3,500 crore. The response was worse on Wednesday with only one bid placed for Rs 200 crore, indicating that the RBI's measure of introducing the 14-day repo facility of Rs 20,000 crore has failed to get the required response.

Golak C Nath, vice-president and economic advisor at Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL), said the Rs 20,000-crore special repo for banks must be kept outside the purview of banks' statutory liquidity requirement if the scheme is to work well. Mutual fund houses largely feel they do not require extra funds. "The latest move will act as a standby credit line for those mutual fund houses that need funds to meet their requirement," Amfi chairman A P Kurien told The Indian Express.

Meanwhile, Indian markets opened sharply lower on downbeat global cues as fears of slowdown in the economy have gripped global markets. Weak cues from European and Asian markets impacted the markets negatively. The broader S&P CNX Nifty of National Stock Exchange was down by 180.25 points, or 5.12 per cent, and ended the day at 3,338.40 points.

All BSE Sectoral indices ended on negative terrain, with consumer durables and capital goods being the worst performer. FIIs were net sellers at Rs 1,030.79 crores on Wednesday, while domestic institutional investors were net buyers at Rs 669.96 crores.

While a survey carried by Crisil on the Indian MF industry stated that fund houses adhered to the basic investment principle of 'buying at low levels' in September 2008, they were net buyers of equity taking advantage of the market slump due to discouraging news from global markets. Crisil Fund Services head Krishnan Sitaraman said, "A predominant portion of the fixed income portfolio of the mutual fund industry is still invested in high quality assets and there is no need to panic on this front. Moreover, the cut in the CRR and the repo facility are expected to improve the situation ."

Heading: PNB cuts home, car loan rates by 0.50% - Indian Express
Content:
The finance ministry estimates that the government will have to infuse about Rs 3,000-4,000 crore in capital into state-owned and public sector banks to help them reach a capital-to-risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) of 12.

According to the Reserve Bank of India, out of 17 nationalised banks (including State Bank of India and its associates) only six have a CRAR below 12 per cent. These are Dena Bank, Andhra Bank, Vijaya Bank, UCO Bank, Union Bank and State Bank of Mysore (see table).

CRAR is the ratio of the capital required to be maintained by the bank to it's risk weighted assets. This indicates the amount of capital to be maintained by a bank to save it from any risk. Finance minister P Chidambaram had today said that the capitalisation plan would be implemented by a suitable date in the future.

All banks in India have a CRAR of over 10 per cent in line with Basel norms of 8 per cent and the RBI's current stipulation of 9 per cent, finance minister P Chidambaram said earlier in the day. The average capital adequacy ratio for scheduled commercial banks, which was around 2 per cent in 1997, had increased to 13.08 per cent as on March 31, 2008. The improvement in the capital adequacy ratio has come about despite significant growth in the aggregate asset of the banking system.

The government has decided to provide banks with access to finance to raise their CRAR and thus bring in more stability in the Indian banking system. This is not the first time banks have been recapitalised in India. Till date, capital in Indian banks has been shored up by over Rs 22,000 crore through recapitalisation bonds.

A finance ministry official said that CRAR of banks could be raised through various means including direct fund infusion in cases where the bank does not have the ability to do so. "Top public sector banks may not need any fund infusion as they have enough head room in tier II loans to raise their CRAR," he said.

Banks could adopt the route of raising equity from the market by way of a follow-on public offer (FPO) or extending preference capital or through various other debt instruments.

Heading: Insurance FDI hike before Cabinet today - Indian Express
Content:
The 2.5 per cent cut in cash reserve ratio (CRR) has started pushing interest rates down. Punjab National Bank on Wednesday decided to reduce the rate of interest by 0.50 per cent on floating rate housing loans and educational loans for existing as well as prospective borrowers. The interest rate will be reduced by 0.50 per cent for the prospective borrowers under fixed rate housing loans and car loans.

"This measure has been taken to ensure credit to borrowers at a lower rate during the festive season. Our bank is the first bank to reduce interest rate on the above loans to pass the benefits to our customers on account of reduction of cash reserve ratio by the Reserve Bank," PNB said. These revised rates will come into effect from October 16.

Further, PNB had increased interest rates on term deposits in various time slabs with peak rate of 10.50 per cent (11 per cent for senior citizens) to pay higher rate of interest to depositors.

The above measures of reduction in rate of interest on retail loans and increase in rate of interest on term deposits along with the benefit due to CRR reduction will be revenue neutral.

On Tuesday, two major state-owned banks — Bank of Baroda and Union Bank of India — had decided to slash rates by 25 basis points on their home loan rates. They are keen to continue with the lower rates even after the festive season if the RBI announces cuts in repo rate and the statutory liquidity rate (SLR) in its forthcoming credit policy on October 24.

Punjab National Bank chairman and managing director K C Chakrabarty said, "It is a welcome step and would ease liquidity pressure. To ensure credit to the borrowers at a lower rate during the festive season we have already cut interest rate in the retail segment even before RBI announced the measure."

In last 10 days, the RBI has announced 2.5 per cent reduction in CRR infusing liquidity to the tune of Rs 1,00,000 crore (around $20 billion) in the cash-starved banking system. Taking into account the Rs 20,000 crore available for mutual funds and the Rs 25,000 crore that came through farm debt waiver scheme, the total fund injection comes to a whopping Rs 1,45,000 crore.

Heading: Vedanta asks Asarco to review purchase price - Indian Express
Content:
The global financial crisis may have hit the world's biggest insurance players severely. But the UPA government is undeterred by the recent turn of events and is hoping to carry forward its financial sector reform agenda, beginning with a hike in foreign direct investment (FDI) limit in the insurance business along with a slew of other reforms.

The Cabinet on Thursday is expected to take up for approval the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Bill that aims to increase the FDI limit in domestic insurance companies to 49 per cent from the existing 26 per cent. The UPA expects to table it in the forthcoming session of Parliament beginning October 17.

The Bill was finally cleared by a GoM led by external affairs minister Pranab Mukherjee last month, over two years after the matter was first referred to it. The GoM has also recommended 10 new provisions in the draft Bill.

Besides increasing FDI, the 60-page draft Bill proposes nearly 120 amendments to insurance laws, including amendments to the Insurance Act of 1938, LIC Act of 1956, and IRDA Act of 1999. A key proposal aims to enable foreign reinsurance firms to enter the market. This would benefit firms like Lloyd's, Munich Re and Swiss Re to get a full branch status in India. Currently state-owned General Insurance Company is the only reinsurer in the country.

(FE)

Heading: Relief will take time, say bush and paulson - Indian Express
Content:
Copper producer Sterlite Ind has asked US-based Asarco LLC, with which it has inked an agreement for a buyout for about $2.6 billion, to review the acquisition price in the wake of the global financial crisis and a fall in the price of the blue metal.

"In view of the recent events affecting the global financial markets and the sudden drop in the price of copper, we had approached Asarco to rediscover the price. They have said they will revert to us," a Sterlite spokesperson said. The spokesperson added the company has secured enough finances for acquiring Asarco.

The clarification from Sterlite on reviewing the buyout price of Asarco comes in the wake of speculation that Vedanta would not be able to pay the offered price due to a severe credit crunch. Last month, the NRI billionaire Anil Agarwal-led Vedanta PLC had called off its corporate restructuring plan citing the turmoil in the global financial markets and adverse feedback from investors.

Meanwhile, with rumours doing the rounds on the Asarco acquisition, the scrip of Sterlite moved southwards to end the day at Rs 292.15, down 10.11 per cent, on the BSE. It had touched an intra-day low of Rs 283.50 and over 26.71 lakh shares of the company changed hands on the bourse.

Heading: Scare in the air - Indian Express
Content:
US President Bush, Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke sought to reassure anxious Americans that relief will come, but it will take time and patience for the plan's unprecedented steps to stabilize the system, induce banks to lend again, and in time help improve the economy. Meanwhile, retail sales in the US fell off a cliff in September, plunging by the largest amount in three years as worried consumers shunned the malls and auto showrooms in the midst of the country's financial meltdown. The Commerce Department reported on Wednesday retail sales decreased 1.2 per cent last month, nearly double the 0.7 per cent drop that had been expected. It was the biggest decline since retail sales fell by 1.4 per cent in August 2005. — AP

ECB unveils measures to boost liquidity

The European Central Bank (ECB) moved Wednesday to make it easier and cheaper for eurozone banks to borrow dollars and Swiss francs, announcing procedural changes that one analyst called "huge". The measures aimed to reduce the costs of borrowing for three and six months that serve as benchmarks for a wide range of lending to business and individuals. "This is extremely important because a lot of loans to corporations and to individuals, mortgages for example, are indexed to these kinds of maturities," Bank of America economist Gilles Moec said. Terming the announcement "huge", Moec said the ECB was trying "to ensure that the interest rate cut last week percolates through the system". — AFP

WB commits $10 bn for Southeast Asia

Philippine President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo has said that the World Bank will contribute $10 billion to a standby facility to assist Southeast Asian countries with severe liquidity problems amid the global financial crisis. "The World Bank indicated that it could initially commit to $10 billion as its contribution to the standby facility," Arroyo said. Arroyo said the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund will draft an implementing mechanism for the standby facility soon after consultations with finance ministers and central bank governors of the 10-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations. "Immediately thereafter, they will convene another meeting to discuss the guidelines for the facility, which we suggested should be quick disbursing with minimal conditions," she said. — PTI

JPMorgan profit sinks, shares fall

JPMorgan Chase & Co's quarterly profit fell 84 per cent, due to mark-downs on underperforming loans, but the results still beat analysts' forecasts. JPMorgan, whose shares slipped 2.5 per cent in pre-market trading, was hit by weakness in its leveraged lending and mortgage-related portfolios, underscoring the strains of the credit crisis. "Given the uncertainty in the capital markets, housing sector and economy overall, it is reasonable to expect reduced earnings for our firm over the next few quarters," Chief Executive Jamie Dimon said in a statement. The bank's adjusted loss of 6 cents per share, before an extraordinary gain related to the acquisition of Washington Mutual's banking operations, beat analyst expectations of a loss of 29 cents per share. — Reuters

World stock markets slip after 2-day rally

European and Asian markets mostly fell back Wednesday following a strong two-day rally. The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was down 145.28 points, or 3.3 percent, at 4,248.93. Germany's DAX was 149.23 points, or 2.9 percent, lower at 5,049.96, while France's CAC-40 was 94.32 points, or 2.6 per cent, down at 3,534.20. In the US, the blue chip Dow Jones Industrial fell by about 200 points in the first 15 minutes of trading, technology stock heavy Nasdaq was down by about 35 points and S&P by more than 28 points. In Asia, Hang Seng Index plummeted nearly five per cent to close at 15,998.30 points. Singapore's Strait Times ended the day down 3.24 per cent at 2,059.39. China's key Shanghai SE Composite IX dropped 1.12 per cent to 1,994.67 points. — AP & PTI

Heading: On the job: Labour ministry jumps into Jet lay-offs mess, trade union cries foul - Indian Express
Content:
For an industry battling losses of $1.5 billion due to high fuel costs, 25-30 per cent over-capacity, dwindling passenger traffic and high taxes, all that civil aviation minister Praful Patel could assure was fight for their cause with the finance ministry and states.

At a closed-door meeting, airline chief executives apprised him of the difficulties they faced in financing aircraft given the reluctance of banks and financial institutions to lend to the sector, now perceived as being risky. This year, they told him the industry was expected to suffer losses of $2 billion.

Patel said the government would look at rationalising the tax structure on aviation turbine fuel. At present, ATF attracts a customs duty of 5.15 per cent and an excise duty of 8.54 per cent. A proposal to put ATF under the declared goods category so that all states levy a uniform 4 per cent sales tax has also been pending with the finance ministry for a while.

States charge between 8 per cent and 34 per cent sales tax on ATF. The issue eluded a consensus at the last meeting of the empowered committee of state finance ministers. Unless all states agree to such a move, it will be difficult to include ATF in the declared goods category.

The minister said he would push for these exemptions in his meeting with finance minister P Chidambaram soon. Airline CEOs also sought the creation of an aviation stabilisation fund, which did not find many takers in the government. "This is difficult," a civil aviation ministry official told The Indian Express. Airlines had earlier too pitched for an interest free loan from the government that could be repaid after three years.

Addressing a press conference on the inaugural day of the India Aviation 2008 event at Hyderabad organised by the ministry and the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Ficci), Patel lashed out at central ministries and states that were still sitting on his proposals. "I am disappointed… Our own oil companies are charging extra prices," he said.

The minister, however, ruled out any likelihood of the government bailing out the private sector. Calling it "unacceptable", he said, "I can't write a cheque directly. The government can, however, certainly look at reducing certain levies such as parking and navigation charges. I will also meet banks and financial institutions to help them (airlines) with working capital and ask them not to put undue pressure on this vital infrastructure sector."

Airlines have also been demanding that the airport landing and route and terminal navigation charges be halved for the next two years. Besides, they have sought a cut in the duty on spare parts for aircraft maintenance and a capping of the airport service charges at current levels. "Some of these are already being considered," said a ministry official.

Heading: How Jet and Kingfisher flew bravely into turbulence - Indian Express
Content:
Holding that sudden sacking of flight attendants by the Jet Airways was "startling" and a "very bad move", the labour ministry today acted swiftly and got in touch with the airline to ascertain the terms of employment of the sacked workers for a possible intervention.

The ministry directed its officials in Mumbai to talk to the airline to find out the status of the sacked employees. "We are trying to find out whether they were regular workers or on contract. Anyways, sacking such a large number of employees at one go is a very bad move," labour secretary Sudha Pillai told The Indian Express.

Sources in the ministry said it was viewing the matter with serious concern and planned to play an active role in the issue after ascertaining the details. "It is a starling move," Pillai added. The ministry is also learnt to be in touch with the civil aviation ministry.

While the labour ministry treaded cautiously, Left-backed trade unions demanded immediate action against the company. "These dismissals are illegal and unwarranted. The CITU demands that the labour ministry direct the company to immediate withdraw these dismissal orders. The CITU further demands that pending such withdrawal of dismissal orders, government should issue orders for grounding all flights of Jet Airways," a statement by the CPI(M)'s trade union arm said. CITU president M K Pandhe, talking to The Indian Express over phone from Kochi, said it was unfortunate that civil aviation minister Praful Patel was siding with the Jet management.

He said the government had already opened its coffers to rescue financial institutions in the wake of global financial meltdown and it could also take some steps like effecting a cut in aviation fuel prices or taxes to help the airlines if they are in distress. "But why sack the workers? What have they done?" said Pandhe.

Pandhe said the Jet Airways was not allowing employees to form unions. "We tried to form a union in Jet, but they removed the workers who came forward."

Heading: The Mohali questionnaire - Indian Express
Content:
'Turbulence Ahead' was the title of the Asia-Pacific outlook for 2008 for the aviation industry by leading market intelligence and analysis agency, the Centre for Asia Pacific Aviation. "2008 is shaping to be one of the most challenging in recent memory for Asia-Pacific aviation as internal and external headwinds blow into the sector," the report had said in its introduction.

Indian aviation analysts and officials think Jet Airways chairman Naresh Goyal and his Kingfisher Airlines counterpart Vijay Mallya either did not give that forecast much attention, or if they did, they didn't take the warnings too seriously -- until this week, that is, when they were forced to join hands to share facilities and cut costs and also lay off employees, in the case of Jet.

The two airlines are the largest full-service private carriers which also own or have merged into themselves low-cost airlines Air Sahara and Air Deccan, cornering a combined 60 per cent share of the Indian market. For most part of this year, Jet and Kingfisher have been on an expansion spree by adding new routes, many of them international for Jet, more employees and more planes even as the overall sector has been taking a beating from soaring global oil prices which led to fare increases and a subsequent fall in the number of passengers.

But with a huge mismatch in operating costs, fare hikes and passenger load factors, Jet and Kingfisher seemed set to emulate state-run Air India which has been way ahead of the rest in terms of losses of more than Rs 2,144 crore in 2007-08 which have been forecast to touch Rs 4,000 crore this year. While Kingfisher posted losses of over Rs 1,000 crore last fiscal, Jet's losses stood at over Rs 800 crore for the same period. And both did not do enough to stem the rot in time, officials said.

"All these carriers have known to operate only in happier times. The aviation industry goes through a cycle of good and bad times every six-seven years, and they seem to be realising this now," said a civil aviation official who did not want to be named. "In the last year or so, 35 airlines have gone bust around the world and that is more than the number that went bust after 9/11. And some of our airlines were expanding mindlessly."

The downturn in the industry this year, officials said, has been sharp and glaring. The fare hikes began reflecting on passenger traffic when the latter declined by 4 per cent in June 2008 over the same month last year, the first such decline in years. It fell a further 12.64 per cent year-on-year in July and another 5.3 per cent sequentially in August. Now, by Jet Airways' own admission, the Indian aviation industry is likely to lose $2 billion in 2008-09.

The crisis in the global financial markets in recent weeks was apparently the wake-up call for the two airlines. With recession staring India in the eye and expected to further hit airline travel, Jet and Kingfisher had no option but to admit that the party was over for now.

While Jet has come out in the open and accepted the crisis by saying that it "expects these difficult market conditions to continue for some time" and that things have reached a "stage at which some hard decisions are inevitable", the industry is now awaiting the moves by Kingfisher and its flamboyant chairman, Vijay Mallya. There is speculation in the industry that Kingfisher is hard on cash and is facing tough times with its vendors for fuel, among others.

But a Kingfisher spokesman denied the talk and said that the airline had a letter of credit for Rs 1,000 crore from ICICI Bank and plans were "pretty much on track". While vendors were being tough across airlines, Kingfisher would do "what it takes to achieve cost efficiencies as the company is ultimately answerable to its shareholders", he said.

Heading: Lee back home for big Test - Indian Express
Content:
Anil Kumble came out for practice on Wednesday but dispelled no doubts over either his form or fitness and, in fact, only intensified speculation over his participation in the second Test with a few minutes of batting.

That the Indian captain has been given time till the morning of the match to take a call on his availability puts the hosts in a quandary over the possible team combination. The Mohali strip traditionally supports seamers, so there is always a temptation to include an extra fast bowler. The question is, in place of whom.

Coach Gary Kirsten, however, will prefer none at the veteran leggie's expense. "We are watching him and at the moment he looks alright. There's a little pain but we hope he'll be ready in two days," Kirsten told mediapersons.

"He is a warrior and is very keen to play. I'm almost sure that regardless of what he is physically, he would be ready to represent the country," said the South African, stressing that Kumble was an experienced bowler and should not judged on the basis of one or two Tests.

"We don't look at one Test, but over a long period of time. Kumble is one of the greatest Indian cricketers ever. A great player struggles (momentarily) before coming back stronger. Kumble has been doing the same for 17 years and I believe he will come up with a match-winning performance here," he said.

The reason behind Kirsten's optimism seems to be the track, as for the first time the word "dry" is being used for the PCA pitch. However, it rained on Wednesday night and it adds to the puzzle. It's hardly a surprise that Kumble spent considerable time with PCA chief curator Daljit Singh.

"We had a look at the pitch, it doesn't have much moisture in it. Actually it looks quite hard and dry. We will have a look again tomorrow and see if playing the third seamer can be a good option," the coach explained.

The curator insisted, as always there would be some assistance for the pacers. Earlier, the Indians arrived at the stadium in the afternoon and spent close to two hours at the nets. The coach sounded happy with the outing, and also with the team's performance in the Bangalore Test.

"I'm very happy with the way we played the first Test. Everyone got some time in the middle. Most made some contributions to the side, it was not big scores but still some sort of contribution and that too in pressure situations.

"Even from my playing days, I have never seen such unity and togetherness in an Indian team. They are eager to win the Test series against Australia," he said.

And the one man he would be pinning his hopes on in Mohali is Zaheer Khan and the coach singled out the left-arm seamer for special praise.

"I think what makes Zaheer such a force is that he has tremendous belief in himself, which helps any player. He is very intelligent too, knows what needs to be done and when. Besides, he has got great variations, knows which ball is to be bowled to which batsman. He is a highly talented bowler," Kirsten said.

But when the Test begins on Friday, it may not be Zaheer or Kumble or anyone else, but Sachin Tendulkar who could walk away with all the limelight. There was glimpse of it as fans scrambled to get a glimpse of the batting maestro, who is just 15 runs short of Brian Lara's record of highest Test aggregate, when he came out practice. Clearly, there is a possibility of the Test getting reduced to a subplot.

Heading: Players cry for rest as domestic grind gets tougher - Indian Express
Content:
For one member of the visiting Australian team, the second Test beginning here on Friday will be more of a home game. Pace spearhead Brett Lee, whose maiden Test appearance on Indian soil fetched him only two wickets, is banking on his IPL experience with Kings XI Punjab to come good at Mohali.

"Sat Sri Akal," Lee greets a group of journalists as he heads for an early practice session at the PCA Stadium. "It's going to be a home game for me and I feel great to come back here," he says before joining the team mates. Lee measures his run-up, a little shorter than usual, but doesn't hold himself back as he hurls the cherry at a trademark express pace. After a long session, Lee, albeit tired, is sporting looks of satisfaction.

"It is only in practice that I bowl from a shorter run-up," says Lee, heading towards the conference room to address the media, and adds what may not be good news for Indian batsmen: "I am happy with the way I am bowling and I am keen to go over 150 kph mark."

However, the fast bowler admits he is still learning how to bowl in Indian conditions and knows he will have to raise his performance several notches higher. "Personally I feel I am still on a learning curve on how to bowl in India. I will be playing only my second Test match in India and I guess it is a tough job.

"Last time, when I toured India with the Test team, I was the twelfth man and this time I am leading the attack; there's a lot of pressure," says Lee, but pins his hope on his previous experience of playing on the PCA track. "I've already played here (in the IPL). It's a great place and hopefully the wicket will have enough carry, especially because this is traditionally a bouncy track. The Bangalore track was slow and the ball stayed low. There was some rain last night and, hopefully, there will be enough bounce for the pacers."

Clark not fit yet

Lee hopes that his new ball partner Stuart Clark will be fit for the Test, but is unsure about his availability. "I'm not going to make any prediction; it is the best left to Alex Kountouris, our physio. The thing is he was in little discomfort and didn't practice today. But we are hoping him to get fit for the second Test. We have got a great side and with Peter Siddle and Doug Boullinger ready to roll their arms, I am sure we don't have to look anywhere else," feels Lee.

Lee also praises Indian pacers Zaheer Khan and Ishant Sharma for the way they bowled in the first Test. "Zaheer and Ishant maintained a good line in Bangalore. Both teams had their chances and if weather had not played its part, we could have won the game. "But in hindsight, we can be happy with the way we played and created chances which will encourage the team a lot in the second Test," asserts Lee.

Heading: Champions Trophy, in a sleek, new version - Indian Express
Content:
While the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) looking forward to the inaugural T20 Champions League in December and the second edition of the Indian Premier League (IPL) next year, their endeavour, on the flipside, has resulted in some thoughtless cramming of the domestic circuit. In order to squeeze the high-profile T20 tournaments in the calendar, the BCCI has shuffled the Ranji fixtures, reducing the usual four-day gap between matches to just three, even as the players are apprehensive about the after-effects of a tight schedule.

Mumbai bowler Avishkar Salvi, easily one of the most injury-prone bowlers in domestic circuit, gives his take on the story. "Three days is a very short time. What if I get injured on the last day of the match, where's the time to recover," he asks. "Now that the schedule has already been announced, we can't help it. All we have to do now is be a lot more cautious, plan it better."

The Mumbai Ranji team suffered quite a bit of injuries last season. Not just Salvi's back injury, Ajit Agarkar and Rajesh Verma too experienced their share of miseries that led to longer period of rests.

"Three days is a really short time. What takes toll on players is traveling. If players are continuously playing at one venue then, at least, things can be taken care of," says Mumbai coach Praveen Amre.

The BCCI, however, says it is helpless with so many tournaments to adjust in a short time frame. "We have to give ten days to the Champions League and that's why we had to shuffle with fixtures. We have a lot of domestic cricket and for every tournament we have allotted a fixed period. If we increase the gap between Ranji matches, the impact will be on all tournaments," says BCCI's Chief Administrative Officer (CAO) Prof Ratanakar Shetty. "People have earlier complained of not getting holidays during Diwali, so we have decided to have off-days during that period."

Saurashtra's Sandeep Jobanputra, who bowled 257 overs in eight matches last season and was the mainstay for his side, says adequate rest is must, and cites his example of missing out on the Ranji one-dayers last season because of excessive workload in the early part of season. "Any fast bowler needs adequate rest and reducing gaps by one day can make a huge difference", he says.

Dr Aijaz Ashai, physiotherapist of the Mumbai team, who also attends to the Indian rugby team, feels that the coming season will be challenging. "Three days aren't enough. If any player has suffered a side strain, he may not get enough time to recover," he says.

After Team India cricketers cried of fatigue and injury due to heavy international commitments, in coming months, players on domestic circuit will lend out similar voices.

Heading: Monty will prepare for India in Lanka - Indian Express
Content:
The International Cricket Council (ICC) on Wednesday re-scheduled the postponed Champions Trophy to September 2009 and will take a final call on the host city after India's tour to Pakistan early next year.

On the final day of a board meeting here, the ICC decided to slot the eight-team event, which was postponed owing to the security apprehensions in Pakistan, from September 24 to October 5.

The board has decided that the tournament will be played in just one city instead of over several venues. "It was further agreed that because the event was reduced in duration (12 days including a reserve day for the final instead of the 17 days) it would be played in one city." "The ICC board will make a final decision on the location of the event following India's tour to Pakistan in the first part of 2009 so that it can provide certainty to teams, broadcasters, commercial partners and other stakeholders.

The ICC decision comes after CEO Haroon Lorgat presented a report on the event's organisation to the board.

"The board received a presentation on the subject in the wake of work carried out by Chief Executive Haroon Lorgat and ICC management. We are delighted to have slotted the ICC Champions Trophy into the FTP in 2009 thus maintaining the primacy of ICC events, and we now look forward to staging it next September-October," ICC president David Morgan said.

The full schedule and the location for the matches will be announced in due course.

Heading: Nadal gets over the edge - Indian Express
Content: Left-arm spinner Monty Panesar is all set for a spell of club cricket in Sri Lanka to sharpen his skills ahead of England's Test series against India in December. Panesar, who will not be part of the England ODI squad ahead of the two Tests in India, will play for Bloomfield club for a month in November before joining the Test team in December. "It's a great opportunity for him. He will learn a lot. But, details have to be finalised to make sure they're happy to have him and he gets the right position," Peter Moores, coach of England team said. "He wants to learn through experience there. There are very good players of spin in Sri Lanka and he will learn a lot. Panesar will team with Sanath Jayasuriya and Tillakaratne Dilshan, who also play for the same club.

Heading: The Bhajji fans from Down Under - Indian Express
Content:
Top seed Rafael Nadal survived a stern test by Latvia's Ernests Gulbis at the Madrid Masters on Tuesday while fourth seed Andy Murray barely broke a sweat as his second-round Italian opponent Simone Bolelli retired hurt.

World number one Nadal showed his trademark tenacity to win 7-5, 3-6, 6-3 in two hours 22 minutes but it could have been very different had Gulbis, ranked 54, held his nerve better.

The 20-year-old from Riga battled gamely with Nadal in the first set but crumbled at 5-5 with double faults and unforced errors to meekly surrender the opening set. Gulbis unleashed blistering shots down both sides of the court in the second, showing why he already has the scalps of American James Blake and Chile's Fernando Gonzalez this year.

His forehand was especially punishing for the French and Wimbledon champion to deal with as were a series of cheeky drop shots that helped the Latvian break Nadal and take the set. But it was the simple shots that ultimately cost Gulbis and after failing to convert a break point against the Spaniard in the third game of the final set, he imploded in the fourth with four unforced errors to effectively hand Nadal the match.

"He played very well in the second set but all the match was very tough because he played very aggressively. You can't get any rhythm. His balls are hit very fast," said Nadal.

The 22-year-old faces 15th seed Richard Gasquet in the third round after the Frenchman beat American Mardy Fish 6-7, 6-4, 6-3.

Easy outing

Murray had a much easier ride in his first outing since losing to Federer in the US Open final five weeks ago, and was leading 6-0 2-1 when world number 43 Bolelli quit. The Italian seemed to injure his shoulder attempting a smash early in the second set and could not battle through the pain. The Scot now meets towering Croat Marin Cilic after the 20-year-old toppled 13th-seeded Madrid local Fernando Verdasco 6-2 6-3.

American James Blake, the 11th seed, was bundled out by Frenchman Gilles Simon 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. Finland's Jarkko Nieminen survived a fightback from Russia's Mikhail Youzhny to win 7-5, 3-6, 6-2 in his first round match.

Heading: Khade starts glory quest - Indian Express
Content:
There's the Indian heat that burns their skin walking the miles around the CYG games village. And there's the man they call the Indian 'hottie,' who is known to get under the skin of their national cricket team. Harbhajan Singh can interpret this epithet bestowed upon him by a gang of chirpy teenaged Australians in Pune any which way he likes. But for these rookie weightlifiters from Queensland and Victoria, the Indian spinner is the character they adore most in Indian cricket.

"Harbhajan's the Indian we enjoy watching the most," starts 17-year-old freckled Steve McConnell, while Sabrina Wheldon chimes in: "He's the best because he causes us the most trouble. Plus, he's always smiling, joking and upto something, getting under our skin, and a good entertainer."

The cricketing caravan in Mohali, though far away from this games village, is big on the minds. "Sachin's a legend, and we love Yuvraj for the way he kills the ball," gushes Emilio McFarland.

The 101-strong Australian contingent saw their swimmers splashing their way up to second on the medals tally, after their hapless lifters and wrestlers had been mauled by the hosts. It was a meteoric rise from afternoon to close of day, when the Aussies climbed up from seventh to second on the overall charts.

The shooting ranges haven't been too bad for the Aussies, with Michael McNabb grabbing the bronze in trap. His father, a rifle shooter himself, opens up to the conversation when cricket comes up. He jokes that shooters from both countries should unite in their grouse against the Big Daddy of the two nation's sports arena. Still, one sniffs a closet admiration for cricket from the tubby man when he speaks of former Aussie captain Mark Taylor. "But tell you what, when Glenn McGrath retired, I lost interest. And the current lot is a little too super-positive," he says.

'Keep it out'

Cringing his long nose, shooting coach Nick Sanders predicts a tough time for the Aussie cricketers on this tour. "We follow the scores on TV, but it's tough to be sitting in India and not stop chanting the obvious: 'We need a spinner'," he says.

Cricket briefly it made to the Commonwealth Games — the senior version — but one of the Empire's grandest sporting imports to the world has failed to make the cut at the youth meet in even its third edition. "Keep it that way — keep it out," quips wrestling coach Fabricio Itte, obviously not a fan. He has an Indian-origin man, Kuldeep Bassi, helping crank up the performance of young Aussie wrestlers back home. Bassi is also taking kabaddi to Australian shores, and Itte insists Indo-Australian sporting contests ought to go beyond the brown wicket and green turf.
